title: "Promptly" is quantified as 1-2 calendar days for derecognition, with good cause required to exceed it
content:
Two Action Tenets attack the same word from different angles. A.1.5.8.0.4.2 glosses "swiftly" qualitatively — "immediate and prompt action without unnecessary delay," because "the urgency is intended to prevent further harm or disruption." A.1.5.9.2.2.0.4.1 goes further and puts a number on "promptly": it "means 'as soon as is reasonably possible,'" and "the Core Facilitator must derecognize the AC within a general timeframe of 1-2 calendar days upon conclusion of an adjudication that finds against the AC for misalignment. Failure to meet this deadline requires a showing of good cause, demonstrating extenuating circumstances beyond the Facilitators' control."

The quantification is the point. A duty to act "promptly" is unenforceable because any given delay can be defended as reasonable; a duty to act within 1-2 days is either met or not. And the burden is deliberately inverted — delay is presumptively a failure that the facilitator must excuse, rather than something a complainant must prove was excessive.

Note precisely where the clock starts: at *conclusion of the adjudication*, not at the allegation. The deadline governs execution of a decision already made, not the investigation itself, which remains bounded only by the qualitative "swiftly" standard. That is a defensible split — investigations legitimately vary in length, while executing a concluded finding does not — but it means the phase with the most discretion is the one without a measurable limit.

The underlying reason for speed is the contagion model in A.1.5.8.0.3.1: a misaligned AC left in place is a vector, so the interval between finding and removal is the actual exposure window.
description: A.1.5.9.2.2.0.4.1 converts a vague urgency standard into a measurable deadline running from the adverse adjudication, and shifts the burden onto the facilitator to justify any delay.
